title: Algebra and functions
text: Original Confine reference, not instructor materials. An equation remains equivalent when the same quantity is added to or subtracted from both sides, or both sides are multiplied by a nonzero quantity. Division by a variable requires checking that it is nonzero. For ax+b=c with a nonzero, x=(c-b)/a. A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. Substitute a value into an expression by replacing every occurrence of its variable. Arithmetic and equivalent algebraic rearrangements are permitted.

title: Derivatives and the chain rule
text: Original Confine reference. The derivative measures instantaneous rate of change: f'(x)=lim as h approaches 0 of (f(x+h)-f(x))/h, when the limit exists. For a positive integer n, d(x^n)/dx=n*x^(n-1). Constants differentiate to zero. Derivatives of sums are sums of derivatives. Product rule: (fg)'=f'g+fg'. Chain rule: d f(g(x))/dx=f'(g(x))*g'(x). Example: d(x^3)/dx=3x^2. Use these rules only when functions are differentiable at the point.

title: Basic integration
text: Original Confine reference. An antiderivative F of f satisfies F'=f. For n not equal to -1, integral x^n dx=x^(n+1)/(n+1)+C on an appropriate domain. Integral 1/x dx=ln|x|+C away from zero. The fundamental theorem gives integral from a to b f(x) dx=F(b)-F(a) for continuous f with antiderivative F. Substitution u=g(x), du=g'(x)dx can change the integral's variable; transform definite limits too. Example: integral 2x dx=x^2+C.

title: Partial derivatives and vectors
text: Original Confine reference. A partial derivative with respect to x differentiates while holding other independent variables constant. For f(x,y)=x^2+y^2, partial f/partial x=2x and partial f/partial y=2y. The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives. The dot product of vectors a and b is the sum of component products. Their Euclidean length is sqrt(sum of squared components). A directional derivative at a differentiable point along a unit vector u is gradient(f) dot u.

title: Counting, permutations, and combinations
text: Original Confine reference. The product rule counts sequences of choices by multiplying numbers of choices at each step when each earlier choice leaves the specified number of later choices. n!=n*(n-1)*...*1, with 0!=1. Ordered selections of k distinct objects from n without replacement number n!/(n-k)!. Unordered selections number choose(n,k)=n!/(k!*(n-k)!). Example: choosing two distinct objects from four gives 4!/(2!*2!)=6. These formulas require integers 0<=k<=n.

title: Logic and induction
text: Original Confine reference. A conjunction p and q is true exactly when both propositions are true. An implication p implies q is false only when p is true and q is false. Its contrapositive, not q implies not p, is equivalent. To prove a statement P(n) by induction for integers n>=n0, establish P(n0) and prove P(k) implies P(k+1) for arbitrary k>=n0. The induction hypothesis assumes only P(k), not the result P(k+1).

title: Recurrences and algorithm growth
text: Original Confine reference. A recurrence defines a quantity using values at smaller indices together with base cases. T(n)=T(n-1)+1 with T(0)=0 gives T(n)=n by repeated substitution. f(n) is O(g(n)) if constants c>0 and n0 exist such that |f(n)|<=c*|g(n)| for all n>=n0. Count operations before assigning a growth class. A loop with n iterations and constant work per iteration takes O(n). No advanced recurrence theorem is included in this reference.

title: Programming foundations
text: Original Confine reference. Variables bind values according to a programming language's types and scope. A conditional selects a branch based on a Boolean condition. A loop repeats its body until its control condition changes; check initialization, termination, and bounds. A function takes inputs and may return a value. Zero-indexed arrays of length n have valid indices 0 through n-1. Trace state changes step by step. This reference does not authorize unmentioned libraries or a different programming language from an assignment.

title: C pointers and memory
text: Original Confine reference. In C, &x obtains the address of object x; *p accesses the object pointed to by a valid pointer p. Declare int *p for a pointer to int. A pointer must refer to a live object before dereference. Local automatic objects cease to exist when their block ends; do not return a pointer to such an object. malloc allocates bytes and can return NULL; test allocation, use sizeof for correct sizes, and free successfully allocated storage exactly once when no longer needed. free does not reset other pointers. Array access must stay within valid bounds. This reference authorizes core C constructs and standard allocation functions only; respect assignment restrictions.

title: C files, compilation, and testing
text: Original Confine reference. C source is compiled into object code and linked into an executable. Headers declare interfaces; source files define functions. FILE* from fopen represents a file stream; check for NULL, use the appropriate read/write operation, and fclose an opened stream. EOF indicates end of input or an error condition; inspect ferror for read errors when needed. Test empty inputs, boundary values, ordinary cases, and error paths. A compiler warning or passing a single test does not establish correctness. Do not execute uploaded code.

title: Probability and conditional probability
text: Original Confine reference. Probabilities are between 0 and 1 and P(sample space)=1. P(A union B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A intersection B). Conditional probability P(A|B)=P(A intersection B)/P(B) for P(B)>0. Independence requires P(A intersection B)=P(A)*P(B). Bayes rule: P(A|B)=P(B|A)*P(A)/P(B). Example: in a fair six-sided die, P(even)=3/6=1/2. Do not assume independence without justification.

title: Binomial and Poisson distributions
text: Original Confine reference. A binomial random variable X counts successes in n independent trials with the same success probability p. P(X=k)=choose(n,k)*p^k*(1-p)^(n-k), for integers 0<=k<=n. choose(n,k)=n!/(k!*(n-k)!). E[X]=n*p and Var(X)=n*p*(1-p). Example: for n=3 and p=0.5, P(X=2)=3*(0.5)^2*(0.5)=0.375. A Poisson variable with parameter lambda>0 has P(X=k)=exp(-lambda)*lambda^k/k!, E[X]=lambda, Var(X)=lambda for nonnegative integers k. State the assumed model.

title: Normal distributions and the central limit theorem
text: Original Confine reference. A normal variable X with mean mu and standard deviation sigma>0 can be standardized as Z=(X-mu)/sigma. Z has standard normal distribution. Probabilities require an approved normal table or a numerical CDF; never invent table values. For independent identically distributed observations with finite mean mu and variance sigma^2, the central limit theorem gives approximate normality of the standardized sample mean as n grows. The standard error of the sample mean is sigma/sqrt(n) when sigma is known. State assumptions and the approximation.

title: Sample summaries and confidence intervals
text: Original Confine reference. The sample mean xbar=(sum of observations)/n. For n>1, sample variance s^2=sum((x_i-xbar)^2)/(n-1). When an independent normal sample has known population standard deviation sigma, a two-sided confidence interval for mu is xbar plus or minus z_(1-alpha/2)*sigma/sqrt(n), using an approved normal quantile. With unknown sigma under the normal model, use the approved Student t quantile with n-1 degrees of freedom and s/sqrt(n). A hypothesis test states a null hypothesis, alternative, significance level, statistic, and model assumptions. A p-value measures extremeness under the null, not the probability the null is true. Obtain critical values or p-values only from provided tables or supported computation; do not invent them.
